blocks.text: Imagine a phone book where you can quickly find any name by opening it roughly in the middle and deciding whether to go left or right. This is the essence of a Binary Search Tree (BST).

blocks.markdown: A Binary Search Tree (BST) is a data structure that maintains elements in a sorted order, allowing for efficient search, insertion, and deletion operations. The key property of a BST is that for any given node, all elements in the left subtree are less than the node, and all elements in the right subtree are greater.

blocks.title: Binary Search Tree Invariant
blocks.text: In a Binary Search Tree, for each node with value \( v \), all values in the left subtree are less than \( v \), and all values in the right subtree are greater than \( v \).

blocks.markdown: Let's explore how this invariant allows us to efficiently search for a key in a BST. When searching for a key, start at the root. If the key equals the root's value, you've found it. If the key is less, move to the left child; if greater, move to the right child. Repeat this process until you find the key or reach a null pointer.

blocks.title: Searching in a BST
blocks.prompt:
Search for the key 15 in the following BST: 

```
      20
     /  \
    10   30
   /  \    \
  5   15   35
```

steps.text: Start at the root node with value 20.
Since 15 < 20, move to the left child with value 10.
Since 15 > 10, move to the right child with value 15.

blocks.answer: The key 15 is found at the right child of node 10.

blocks.markdown: Insertion in a BST also relies on the invariant. To insert a new key, follow the same path as the search operation until reaching a null pointer, where the new node is inserted. This maintains the BST property.

blocks.title: Inserting a Node in a BST
blocks.prompt:
Insert the key 25 into the following BST: 

```
      20
     /  \
    10   30
   /  \    \
  5   15   35
```

steps.text: Start at the root node with value 20.
Since 25 > 20, move to the right child with value 30.
Since 25 < 30, move to the left child, which is null.
Insert the new node with value 25 as the left child of node 30.

blocks.answer: The key 25 is inserted as the left child of node 30.

blocks.markdown: Deletion in a BST is more complex, particularly when the node to be deleted has two children. The general strategy is to replace the node with its in-order predecessor (maximum of the left subtree) or in-order successor (minimum of the right subtree) to maintain the invariant.

blocks.caption: Time complexities of operations on a BST. The worst-case occurs when the tree degenerates into a linked list.

blocks.markdown: The efficiency of a BST heavily depends on its height. Ideally, a BST is balanced, with a height of \(O(\log n)\). However, if nodes are inserted in a sorted order, the tree can degenerate into a linked list with a height of \(O(n)\), leading to inefficient operations.

blocks.title: Degeneration of BST
blocks.text: A BST can degenerate into a linked list if elements are inserted in a sorted order, resulting in \(O(n)\) time complexity for search, insertion, and deletion.

points: A BST maintains a sorted order using the invariant that left children are less and right children are greater.
Search, insertion, and deletion operations in a BST have average time complexities of \(O(\log n)\) but can degrade to \(O(n)\) in the worst case.
The order of insertion affects the efficiency of a BST, with sorted insertions leading to degeneration.
